newsitem.title: USA: Glickman does not see N Korea as big ag purchaser.
newsitem.headline: Glickman does not see N Korea as big ag purchaser.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday that North Korea's economic problems will limit how much grain it can commercially purchase from the United States, but he said it will likely continue to be a recipient of U.S. food aid for some time.

"I don't see North Korea as a big purchasing nation ... but I see it as a recipient nation for a while," Glickman told reporters when asked if he viewed North Korea as a potential market for U.S. commodities in light of the recent wheat deal Cargill grain company just worked out with it.
Glickman spoke to reporters after addressing a rural youth organization national conference.

Cargill announced Monday that after three months of negotiations, it would be making a commercial wheat sale to North Korea. Korean sources said the arrangement was a barter deal with Cargill swapping some 20,000 tonnes of wheat for 4,000 tonnes of zinc. Cargill has been approved to sell 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to North Korea, and a Cargill official said the company would continue working with North Korea to develop more transactions.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters Tuesday the adminstration is "seriously reviewing" the latest appeal made last week by the U.N. World Food Program for an extra $95.5 million to help North Korea cope with serious food shortages.

Glickman noted dire comments made Tuesday from democrat congresman Tony Hall of Ohio after a recent trip to North Korea on the severity of the food crisis in the country. Hall called the situation a "hell of severe famine."
The Agriculture Secretary indicated that he would support more food aid to North Korea, and said, "We in this country obviously have had a long history in fighting hunger wherever it exists."
